sources.title: GitHub CLI
sources.credibility_signals: Official GitHub CLI organization repository; MIT licensed; mature cross-platform authentication implementation.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-07-22; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Provides a production reference for device/web OAuth orchestration, multiple accounts, secure-store references, logout, and bounded keyring calls.
sources.key_finding: The CLI selects device or web authorization, validates the browser URL, presents one-time codes, stores secrets in a keyring, and keeps non-secret account configuration separate.
sources.implementation_implication: Reference its provider/account state separation and bounded secure-store operations; browser and device flows remain provider capabilities rather than universal fallbacks.

sources.title: GitHub CLI OAuth library
sources.credibility_signals: Maintained by the official GitHub CLI organization; MIT licensed; used by GitHub CLI.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-07-21; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Compact production example of RFC 8628 device authorization and localhost browser authorization for a CLI.
sources.key_finding: The library supports device authorization and a localhost web-flow fallback while explicitly limiting its provider-compatibility claims.
sources.implementation_implication: Select flows from a typed provider capability declaration and retain provider-specific conformance tests; do not infer support from library capability alone.
sources.selection_note: Excluded to avoid duplicating the mature GitHub CLI implementation; it adds no distinct Task 19A decision evidence.

sources.title: Git Credential Manager
sources.credibility_signals: Maintained under the Git ecosystem organization; broad production use; repository README states MIT licensing.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-07-20 and a 2026 release; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Documents real cross-platform credential-store behavior and browser/device authorization choices, including Linux and headless limitations.
sources.key_finding: Native macOS and Windows stores are available, Linux has multiple non-equivalent backends and no universal default, and Secret Service may require an unlocked GUI session; plaintext is explicitly insecure.
sources.implementation_implication: Model secure-store availability and lock/prompt state explicitly. Require a supported backend or deliberate encrypted fallback, never silent plaintext storage.

sources.title: keyring-rs
sources.credibility_signals: Maintained upstream project with native macOS, Windows, and Unix-store backends; Apache-2.0/MIT licensing.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-07-20; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Most directly relevant Rust integration candidate for native secure-store set/get/delete operations without introducing a mandatory service.
sources.key_finding: The project supports text and binary secrets in platform-native stores and permits selecting specific store backends rather than enabling every implementation.
sources.implementation_implication: Compile only supported platform backends, probe the actual store, keep opaque entry IDs in SQLite, and treat delete failures as lifecycle errors.

sources.title: oauth2-rs
sources.credibility_signals: Mature typed Rust OAuth library; Apache-2.0/MIT licensing; supports major OAuth protocol extensions.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed 2026 activity; reviewed source revision 72ce74401c26eb4dc85dcbfde587bbcfc149e3ae on 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Provides Rust-native authorization-code/PKCE, device authorization, introspection, and revocation primitives suitable for an adapter policy layer.
sources.key_finding: Its device-flow implementation handles polling interval, authorization-pending, slow-down, expiration, and timeout semantics; no complete provider onboarding or DCR policy layer is implied.
sources.implementation_implication: Use protocol primitives behind endpoint/issuer allowlists, strict scopes, cancellation, redirect binding, and provider capability checks.

sources.title: AppAuth for Android
sources.credibility_signals: OpenID Foundation repository; Apache-2.0 licensed; widely used native-app OAuth/OIDC implementation.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity in 2026; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Primary implementation reference for external-browser PKCE, authorization state, metadata discovery, and RFC 7591 registration semantics.
sources.key_finding: The library uses external browsers and PKCE, does not support WebView authorization, and performs dynamic client registration only against an advertised or configured registration endpoint.
sources.implementation_implication: Use its state machine as a design reference, not a Rust dependency. Never embed a static client secret as if a native executable could keep it confidential.
sources.selection_note: Excluded because the Android-specific implementation is outside the local Rust desktop/CLI delivery surface.

sources.title: Coinbase Advanced Python SDK
sources.credibility_signals: Published by the official Coinbase organization; Apache-2.0 licensed; provider-maintained Advanced Trade implementation.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-06-19; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Confirms the production boundary between no-auth public clients and authenticated clients that consume an already issued key.
sources.key_finding: Public endpoints can be used without credentials; authenticated SDK construction requires a key created through the provider portal and does not issue that key.
sources.implementation_implication: Offer no-credential Coinbase market-data onboarding by default; private access is manual-key import, secure storage, and permission verification.
sources.selection_note: Excluded because official Coinbase documentation is stronger for the no-auth/authenticated boundary and the Python SDK adds no issuance capability.

sources.title: Kraken CLI
sources.credibility_signals: Published by the official Kraken organization; MIT licensed; Rust CLI for public, private, and paper workflows.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-04-20; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Shows the provider-supported public/paper no-key path and the exact boundary where a human-created private key is consumed.
sources.key_finding: Public and paper commands require no credential; private setup imports keys created in Kraken settings and protects local configuration but does not issue keys.
sources.implementation_implication: Default to no-key modes; import a least-privilege private key only when requested and store it in the OS keyring rather than duplicating file-secret storage.

sources.title: Docker credential helpers
sources.credibility_signals: Official Docker organization repository; MIT licensed; production backends for macOS, Windows, Secret Service, and pass.
sources.freshness_signals: Public GitHub metadata showed activity through 2026-07-21; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Demonstrates a small stable helper contract separated from platform-specific secure-store implementations.
sources.key_finding: A narrow get/store/erase contract can isolate native credential backends without exposing a general shell or filesystem interface.
sources.implementation_implication: Reference the backend boundary for a Market Squawk credential-store trait or optional helper while retaining a native, no-mandatory-runtime baseline.
sources.selection_note: Excluded because keyring-rs and Git Credential Manager cover the relevant cross-platform secure-store contract more directly.

sources.title: RustCrypto zeroize
sources.credibility_signals: Maintained by RustCrypto; package is Apache-2.0/MIT licensed; established explicit-zeroing implementation.
sources.freshness_signals: Parent repository public metadata showed activity through 2026-07-22; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Directly supports short-lived secret-buffer hygiene at the provider/keyring boundary.
sources.key_finding: The crate provides compiler-resistant explicit zeroing and does not silently substitute an ineffective implementation.
sources.implementation_implication: Redact and zeroize secret-bearing buffers after exchange or secure-store insertion; treat this as defense in depth, not persistent storage.
sources.selection_note: Excluded from this architectural decision because zeroization is already an admitted repository dependency and does not decide provider onboarding mode.

sources.title: RFC 8252: OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps
sources.credibility_signals: IETF consensus Best Current Practice for native-app OAuth; published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published October 2017; remains the native-app BCP; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Defines the portal's browser and PKCE boundary for installed applications.
sources.key_finding: Native apps use an external user agent, public clients use PKCE, and embedded user agents are prohibited.
sources.implementation_implication: Use the system browser plus exact loopback/app redirects, state, and PKCE; do not embed provider login or promise invisible authorization.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 8628: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
sources.credibility_signals: IETF standards-track protocol published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published August 2019; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Defines the only standard browser-on-another-device flow relevant to a local CLI/portal.
sources.key_finding: The protocol defines device/user codes, verification URIs, polling intervals, pending and slow-down responses, expiration, and explicit user approval.
sources.implementation_implication: Enable only for providers that advertise support and implement bounded, cancellable, expiration-aware polling with required backoff.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 7591: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration
sources.credibility_signals: IETF standards-track protocol published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published July 2015; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Defines what OAuth client-registration automation can and cannot accomplish.
sources.key_finding: A registration endpoint accepts client metadata and returns a client identifier and possible credentials; it may require an initial access token.
sources.implementation_implication: Represent DCR as optional OAuth client provisioning, never as provider user-account or personal API-key creation.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 7592: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management
sources.credibility_signals: IETF-published Experimental protocol for registration management.
sources.freshness_signals: Published July 2015; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Covers lifecycle operations after dynamic client registration, including deletion and rotation.
sources.key_finding: Defines read, update, and delete of client registrations plus registration access tokens and credential rotation.
sources.implementation_implication: Use only where explicitly supported, secure the management token, and preserve the RFC's Experimental status in architecture decisions.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 8414: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata
sources.credibility_signals: IETF standards-track discovery protocol published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published June 2018; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Defines authenticated discovery inputs for issuer, endpoints, capabilities, and optional registration endpoint.
sources.key_finding: Authorization-server metadata is fetched from a well-known location and its returned issuer must exactly match the issuer used to construct the request.
sources.implementation_implication: Fetch only from allowlisted HTTPS issuers, require exact issuer matching, and reject or audit unexpected endpoint/configuration drift.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 9700 / BCP 240: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
sources.credibility_signals: Current IETF OAuth security BCP; consensus-reviewed and published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published January 2025; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Current baseline for OAuth threat mitigations and deprecated modes.
sources.key_finding: Updates OAuth threat guidance, deprecates insecure modes, and strengthens redirect, authorization-code, scope, and token-handling requirements.
sources.implementation_implication: Use authorization code plus PKCE, exact redirects, strict state/issuer binding, minimum scopes, and supported refresh protections; exclude legacy implicit/password flows.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: RFC 7009: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation
sources.credibility_signals: IETF standards-track token lifecycle protocol published by the RFC Editor.
sources.freshness_signals: Published August 2013; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Defines the remote credential closeout operation required for complete deactivation.
sources.key_finding: Defines token revocation and requires clients to tolerate token invalidation; refresh-token revocation is part of the authorization-server lifecycle surface.
sources.implementation_implication: Attempt and audit remote revocation where supported before deleting the local secure-store entry; local deletion alone does not revoke provider authority.
sources.selection_note: Reclassified from papers discovery to official documentation because an RFC is a normative standard, not an academic paper.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Digital Identity Guidelines — Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.credibility_signals: Final NIST Special Publication by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
sources.freshness_signals: Published August 2025; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Supplies current authentication and authenticator-lifecycle guidance for sensitive local portal actions.
sources.key_finding: Defines lifecycle and assurance considerations for authentication and authenticator management.
sources.implementation_implication: Apply lifecycle controls and reauthentication to sensitive local actions, but do not label provider API keys as human authenticators or claim an assurance level without the full profile.
sources.selection_note: Excluded from the academic-paper lane because it is a government standard, not empirical or formal research; REP-003 covers it in reputable sources.

sources.title: A Comprehensive Formal Security Analysis of OAuth 2.0
sources.credibility_signals: Original work by Daniel Fett, Ralf Küsters, and Guido Schmitz with a formal web model and proofs.
sources.freshness_signals: Published 2016; foundational attack/proof analysis; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Provides rigorous evidence that individually familiar OAuth checks are insufficient without complete participant and session binding.
sources.key_finding: The analysis identified attacks in common OAuth deployments and proved a corrected profile only with a complete set of protocol recommendations.
sources.implementation_implication: Implement authorization as a typed state machine binding provider, issuer, redirect, state, authorization code, and local session rather than hand-written callbacks.

sources.title: Universal Cross-app Attacks: Exploiting and Securing OAuth 2.0 in Integration Platforms
sources.credibility_signals: Published in the USENIX Security 2025 technical program with original empirical platform analysis.
sources.freshness_signals: Published 2025; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Directly studies multi-provider integration platforms, the closest architectural analogue to the portal.
sources.key_finding: Across 18 integration platforms, the study found cross-app token and request-forgery classes caused by insufficient differentiation between applications and authorization transactions.
sources.implementation_implication: Namespace and bind callbacks and pending state by provider, adapter, account, client, redirect URI, and one-time transaction; never share an ambiguous callback/token slot.

sources.title: Inconsistent, Incomplete, and Insecure: A Survey of Account Security Interfaces
sources.credibility_signals: Accepted in the USENIX Security 2026 technical program; original study of 100 service security interfaces.
sources.freshness_signals: 2026 accepted/prepublication material; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Evidence for conservative provenance and credential-activity UI claims.
sources.key_finding: The study reports inconsistent access disclosure and many spoofable or misleading device/location descriptions across major services.
sources.implementation_implication: Show only evidence-backed provider, credential, scope, secure-store, and lifecycle facts; avoid overclaiming device or location provenance.
sources.selection_note: Excluded because it was prepublication evidence and the accepted 2025 integration-platform study more directly supports the portal threat model.

sources.title: An Extensive Formal Security Analysis of the OpenID Financial-grade API
sources.credibility_signals: Original formal analysis by Daniel Fett, Pedram Hosseyni, and Ralf Küsters of a financial-grade authorization profile.
sources.freshness_signals: Published 2019; retrieved 2026-07-22.
sources.selection_rationale: Financial-domain evidence that a high-assurance profile must be adopted as a coherent protocol, not as isolated controls.
sources.key_finding: The formal analysis found attacks even in a hardened financial API profile before specifying mitigations and proving the corrected design.
sources.implementation_implication: If broker OAuth or execution authority is added, adopt a complete supported high-assurance profile and conformance suite instead of composing selected safeguards ad hoc.
